tech-linux-tickets.title: Linux Real-World Ticket Queue
tech-linux-tickets.description: Thirty realistic Linux support tickets in six queues — disk 100%, service won't start, permission denied, high load, can't SSH and expired certificates — each with investigation (including red herrings), diagnosis, ordered resolution and an ITIL-style closure note, plus simulated consoles for the capstones. Invented hosts and IPs; independent material.

courses.title: Ticket queue I · Disk 100%
courses.summary: Five realistic disk-full tickets: remote log growth, container storage, inode floods, /boot full and a P1 database disk — each with investigation, diagnosis, resolution and closure notes. Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current skills outline.
outcomes: Learners can triage disk-full alerts across very different causes
Learners can choose safe, reversible fixes
Learners can write professional closure notes
Learners can separate incident fix from problem prevention

lessons.title: Lab: /var full on a log server

scenes.text: Ticket queue: 'log01 alerts /var 100%'.
Riya takes it.

steps.title: Disk-full method
steps.body: df → du drill-down (-x) → identify owner/purpose → safe action (truncate/compress/move/extend) → root-cause fix → alerting.

steps.title: Senior tip
steps.body: Ask 'who writes this and why did it grow now?' — the growth trigger is the root cause.

steps.title: Ticket hygiene (ITIL vocabulary)
steps.body:
- Acknowledge within SLA, set the right priority (impact × urgency)
- Work notes: what you checked, what you found, what you changed — with timestamps
- Restore service first (Incident), then remove root cause (Problem); risky fixes go through Change
- Closure note: root cause, fix, verification, prevention

ticket.description: Automated alert: filesystem /var used 100% (threshold 90%). rsyslog queue warnings.

investigate.label: ls -lh /var/log/remote/fw-edge01/ | tail -2
investigate.reveal: -rw------- 1 root root 79G Nov 26 11:58 messages (no rotation for remote dir)

options: Remote logs from fw-edge01 (debug level enabled) aren't covered by logrotate
diagnosis.why: One remote host's log grew to 79G in an unrotated directory.

resolution: Compress/move older remote logs to archive to free space now
Ask network team to reduce fw-edge01 logging from debug
Add logrotate rule for /var/log/remote/*/*
Verify df and rsyslog queue drained
Raise Problem for capacity alerts per remote host

closure.model: Root cause: /var/log/remote not covered by logrotate; fw-edge01 switched to debug on 24 Nov producing 79G. Freed 70G by compressing to /archive; network team reverted logging to info (CHG0101700); logrotate rule added (daily, rotate 30, compress). /var now 31%, rsyslog queue empty.

quiz.q: Why include remote logs in logrotate?
quiz.why: Correct answer: Otherwise they grow unbounded.
Correct answer: Compress/move old remote logs.
Correct answer: Rotation + per-source volume alerting.

lessons.title: Lab: Docker/Podman storage ate the root disk

scenes.text: ci10 builds fail: 'no space left on device'.
Images and build cache pile up.

steps.title: Container storage
steps.body: `podman system df` / `docker system df` → prune dangling images, stopped containers, build cache per policy → move storage to a dedicated volume.

steps.title: Senior tip
steps.body: Schedule prune jobs on CI runners; never prune on prod hosts without checking what's in use.

steps.title: Ticket hygiene (ITIL vocabulary)
steps.body:
- Acknowledge within SLA, set the right priority (impact × urgency)
- Work notes: what you checked, what you found, what you changed — with timestamps
- Restore service first (Incident), then remove root cause (Problem); risky fixes go through Change
- Closure note: root cause, fix, verification, prevention

ticket.description: All pipelines on ci10 fail at 'docker build' with no space left. Pls fix.

investigate.label: docker system df
investigate.reveal: Images 412 (reclaimable 61G)  Build Cache 14G reclaimable  Containers 88 stopped

options: Unpruned images, stopped containers and build cache accumulated in /var/lib/docker on the root fs

resolution: docker container prune -f (stopped CI containers)
docker image prune -a --filter 'until=168h' -f
docker builder prune --filter 'until=72h' -f
Verify df and rerun a pipeline
Add a nightly prune timer and move /var/lib/docker to a dedicated volume (Change)

closure.model: Root cause: no cleanup on CI runner; /var/lib/docker (76G) on root fs. Pruned stopped containers, images >7 days, build cache >3 days — freed 68G; pipelines green. Nightly prune timer added; CHG0101720 to move docker storage to /dev/sdb.

options: Container growth shouldn't fill the OS filesystem
quiz.why: Correct answer: Container growth shouldn't fill the OS filesystem.

options: Only after checking what's in use/needed
quiz.why: Correct answer: Only after checking what's in use/needed.

Inodes again.

ticket.description: Users say emails are not going out since 2am. Server shows no space but disk isn't full??

investigate.label: Sample queued message
investigate.reveal: From: noreply@app-legacy01 To: invalid@… — loop of bounce notifications

options: app-legacy01 generated a bounce loop flooding the Postfix queue, exhausting inodes

resolution: Block/relay-deny app-legacy01 temporarily
Delete its queued messages: postsuper -d with a filtered queue ID list
Confirm inodes freed (df -i)
Flush legitimate queue: postqueue -f
Raise Problem with app owner to fix the loop

closure.model: Root cause: app-legacy01 bounce loop created 1.9M queued messages (inodes 100%). Temporarily blocked source, removed its messages with postsuper -d (filtered list), inodes 22%, legit queue flushed 10:12. PRB0004450 with app owner.

quiz.why: Correct answer: Otherwise it refills immediately.

scenes.text: Patching app19 failed: /boot has no space.
Old kernels.

steps.title: /boot
steps.body: List installed kernels → keep running + previous → remove extras with the package manager → set installonly_limit → retry update.

steps.title: Senior tip
steps.body: Never delete files in /boot by hand; use dnf/apt so GRUB entries stay consistent.

ticket.description: Automated patch job: Error: Transaction test error: installing package kernel-core… needs 48MB more space on the /boot filesystem

options: Too many old kernels retained (installonly_limit raised to 6 previously) filling /boot

resolution: Confirm running kernel with uname -r
dnf remove --oldinstallonly --setopt installonly_limit=2 kernel
Set installonly_limit=3 in /etc/dnf/dnf.conf
Re-run dnf upgrade
Reboot in window and verify new kernel

closure.model: Root cause: installonly_limit=6 retained 6 kernels; /boot 97%. Removed old kernels keeping running+previous, set installonly_limit=3, update succeeded; rebooted 22:40 into 5.14.0-503.16.1; /boot 46%.

options: Leaves package DB and bootloader entries inconsistent
quiz.why: Correct answer: Leaves package DB and bootloader entries inconsistent.

Data files must not be touched.

steps.title: DB disk-full rules

- Never delete data/ibdata/redo files
- Usual safe levers: purge binary logs already replicated/backed up (`PURGE BINARY LOGS BEFORE …`), remove old dumps, extend LV
- Check replicas before purging binlogs

ticket.description: Checkout throws 'database is read only' / 'Disk full (/var/lib/mysql)'. URGENT.

investigate.label: SHOW REPLICA STATUS on db15
investigate.reveal: Relay_Master_Log_File: binlog.004812 — replica up to date

investigate.label: Restart MariaDB
investigate.reveal: Not tried — would not free space and risks recovery time.

options: expire_logs_days was unset, so binlogs accumulated (212G); purge binlogs older than the replica's position and set retention
diagnosis.why: Binlogs without retention; replica confirms which can be purged.

resolution: Confirm replica position and last backup includes binlogs
PURGE BINARY LOGS TO 'binlog.004700' (safely behind replica)
Verify free space and writes resume
Set binlog_expire_logs_seconds (e.g. 7 days) persistently
Raise Change to add disk to vgdb; Problem record for capacity monitoring

closure.model: Root cause: no binlog retention configured; binlogs reached 212G filling /var/lib/mysql. After confirming replica db15 at binlog.004812 and backup coverage, ran PURGE BINARY LOGS TO 'binlog.004700' freeing 190G; writes resumed 12:41. Set binlog_expire_logs_seconds=604800; CHG0101850 adds 250G to vgdb.

terminal.prompt: Free space safely using the DB's own command.

responses.out: /dev/mapper/vgdb-data  500G  310G  191G  62% /var/lib/mysql

lessons.title: Lab: Typo in config after a change

scenes.text: After a deploy, nginx is down on web15.
status, journal, -t.

steps.title: Service start triage
steps.body: systemctl status → journalctl -u -b → service's own config test → recent changes (dnf history, git log, change tickets).

steps.title: Senior tip
steps.body: Ask 'what changed?' first — most failures follow a change.

ticket.description: We deployed the new vhost at 18:05 and now nothing loads. Rolled back code but still down.

investigate.label: Rollback code again
investigate.reveal: Config isn't part of the code repo; no change.

options: Typo 'proxy_passs' in the new vhost config, outside the code rollback
diagnosis.why: nginx -t / journal names the exact line.

resolution: Fix the typo in new.conf line 14
nginx -t
systemctl start nginx
Verify site and add nginx -t to the deploy pipeline

closure.model: Root cause: typo 'proxy_passs' in /etc/nginx/conf.d/new.conf:14 introduced at 18:05 (config not in code rollback). Fixed, nginx -t OK, started 18:31, site verified. Pipeline now runs nginx -t before reload.

quiz.q: Why did code rollback not help?
options: The broken file wasn't part of the code
quiz.why: Correct answer: The broken file wasn't part of the code.

options: Validate config in the pipeline before reload
quiz.why: Correct answer: Validate config in the pipeline before reload.

ticket.description: billing.service fails since monitoring agent was installed this morning.

investigate.label: journalctl -u billing -b
investigate.reveal: java.net.BindException: Address already in use (Bind failed) on 0.0.0.0:9100

options: New node_exporter (default 9100) collides with billing's metrics port 9100

resolution: Agree with monitoring team which service moves
Change billing metrics port to 9101 (or node_exporter --web.listen-address)
Restart billing; verify
Update firewall/monitoring targets
Record port allocation in CMDB

closure.model: Root cause: node_exporter installed 09:10 listens on 9100, same as billing's metrics port. Moved billing metrics to 9101 (CHG0101900), billing started 10:02, Prometheus targets updated. Port registry updated in CMDB.

quiz.why: Correct answer: Another process owns the port.

scenes.text: reports.service fails, but the dev can run it in his shell.
systemd's environment is not your shell's.

steps.title: Environment differences
steps.body: Compare the unit's User/WorkingDirectory/Environment with the dev's shell; check ExecStart path (203/EXEC), missing files (EnvironmentFile), venv paths.

steps.title: Senior tip
steps.body: `systemd-run --uid=app --pty /path/to/cmd` reproduces systemd's environment interactively.

ticket.description: reports.service failed last night. I can run 'python3 run.py' fine myself.

options: Unit uses system python3 instead of the project venv where pandas is installed
diagnosis.why: Shell activates the venv; systemd doesn't.

resolution: Change ExecStart to /opt/reports/venv/bin/python3 /opt/reports/run.py
systemctl daemon-reload
systemctl start reports and check journal
Add a dependency check to the deploy

closure.model: Root cause: reports.service ExecStart used /usr/bin/python3; dependencies live in /opt/reports/venv (activated only in the dev's .bashrc). ExecStart updated to the venv interpreter, daemon-reload, manual run OK 09:20; tonight's run monitored.

quiz.why: Correct answer: ExecStart binary missing/not executable.

lessons.title: Lab: Start timeout and dependency failures

scenes.text: app21's service times out after 90 s at boot.
It depends on an NFS mount that isn't ready.

steps.title: Ordering and timeouts
steps.body: `systemctl list-dependencies`, `systemd-analyze critical-chain unit`, look for 'start operation timed out' and 'Dependency failed'. Use RequiresMountsFor=/After= correctly.

steps.title: Senior tip
steps.body: `systemd-analyze blame` lists slow units at boot.

ticket.description: After patch reboot the media app didn't come up. Starting it by hand later works.

investigate.label: journalctl -b -u media
investigate.reveal: media.service: start operation timed out. Terminating. — app waited for /srv/media files

investigate.label: journalctl -b -u srv-media.mount
investigate.reveal: Mounted /srv/media at 06:04:31 (2 min after media.service started)

options: media.service isn't ordered after the NFS mount, so at boot it starts before /srv/media exists

resolution: Add RequiresMountsFor=/srv/media to [Unit]
systemctl daemon-reload
Reboot test in window
Verify media starts after mount (systemd-analyze critical-chain media.service)

closure.model: Root cause: media.service only had After=network.target and started before the NFS mount /srv/media, timing out. Added RequiresMountsFor=/srv/media; reboot test 22:10 OK, critical-chain shows mount → media.

ticket.short: Can't SSH to bastion02 — all prod access blocked
ticket.description: Nobody can reach bastion02 since the 14:00 hardening push. We have no other way into prod!

options: Invalid cipher names in the hardening drop-in (missing '@openssh.com' suffix) make sshd refuse to start
diagnosis.why: sshd -t reports a bad cipher spec in the new drop-in.

resolution: From console, correct Ciphers to chacha20-poly1305@openssh.com,aes256-gcm@openssh.com
sshd -t returns clean
systemctl restart sshd
Test SSH from another host
Fix the hardening template and add sshd -t to the pipeline; review change CHG0101950

closure.model: Root cause: hardening drop-in (CHG0101950) listed ciphers without '@openssh.com' suffix; sshd -t: bad cipher spec, so sshd failed to start. Fixed via VM console, sshd -t clean, restarted 14:36, SSH verified from jump01. Template corrected and pipeline now runs sshd -t.

scenes.text: Two new finance hires can't write to /srv/finance.
Groups and login sessions.

steps.title: Permission denied method
steps.body: Identify the exact path + operation + user → `id user`, `namei -l path`, `getfacl`, `ls -Z` → SELinux denials (`ausearch -m AVC`) → fix the least-privilege way.

steps.title: Senior tip
steps.body: Group changes apply at next login — ask the user to log out/in (or `newgrp`).

ticket.short: New joiners can't save to Finance share
ticket.description: Hi, Ravi and Kavya joined Monday, they can open files in /srv/finance but get 'permission denied' when saving. Others are fine.

investigate.label: getfacl /srv/finance | grep ravi
investigate.reveal: user:ravi:r-x (temporary read ACL added by helpdesk)

options: Joiners weren't added to the finance group; a helpdesk ACL gave them read only

resolution: Get approval from the finance manager (data owner)
usermod -aG finance ravi; usermod -aG finance kavya
Remove the temporary read ACLs (setfacl -x u:ravi …)
Ask users to log out/in and test saving
Close with approval reference

closure.model: Approved by Lata (data owner). Added ravi and kavya to group finance; removed temporary read-only ACLs. Users re-logged in and saved test files 11:20. Ticket closed.

quiz.why: Correct answer: At next login (or newgrp).

options: Avoid privilege creep and confusing overlaps
quiz.why: Correct answer: Avoid privilege creep and confusing overlaps.

ticket.description: Since yesterday's restore, product images show broken icons. Text pages fine.

options: Restored files carry default_t label instead of httpd_sys_content_t

resolution: restorecon -Rv /var/www/uploads
Retest image URLs
Fix the restore procedure to preserve contexts (tar --selinux / rsync -X) or run restorecon after restore
Close

lessons.title: Lab: Script fails with 'Permission denied' in cron

scenes.text: A newly deployed /opt/tools/sync.sh fails in cron.
Mount options and exec bit.

steps.title: Execution denied
steps.body: Check exec bit (`ls -l`), interpreter line, mount options (`findmnt -T path` for noexec), SELinux type (`bin_t` vs `user_home_t`), and the user cron runs as.

steps.title: Senior tip
steps.body: noexec mounts (e.g. /tmp, /home on hardened builds) block direct execution — `bash script.sh` works but is a workaround, not a fix.

ticket.description: The new sync job doesn't run from cron. In my terminal 'bash sync.sh' works.

options: /home is mounted noexec by the hardening baseline; the script lives in a home dir

resolution: Move the script to /opt/tools (exec allowed) owned by a service account
Set mode 750, correct SELinux type (restorecon)
Update crontab path
Verify next run in cron log

closure.model: Root cause: /home is mounted noexec (hardening baseline) so cron couldn't execute /home/joel/tools/sync.sh. Moved to /opt/tools/sync.sh (svc-sync:svc-sync, 750), crontab updated; 14:00 run successful in cron log.

investigate.label: ls -l /var/log/orders
investigate.reveal: -rw-r--r-- root root app.log (created by deploy script run as root)

scenes.text: Ravi, a Java developer, opens main.dart and writes `String name = 'Asha';`. It works, but his teammate says 'we usually write final here'.
He wonders when to use var, final or const — and why Dart is so strict about them.

steps.title: var, final, const
steps.body:
- **var** lets the compiler infer the type; the variable can be reassigned (but not to a different type).
- **final** is assigned once at runtime and never again.
- **const** is a compile-time constant: the value must be known when the program is compiled.

`final now = DateTime.now();` is legal (known only at runtime). `const now = DateTime.now();` is a compile error.

steps.title: Read this code
Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking final means the object is immutable: a final List can still have items added; only the variable cannot be reassigned.
- Using const for values computed at runtime.
- Using `dynamic` to escape the type checker: you lose compile-time safety.

scenes.text: A cart app splits 7 items into 2 boxes and shows '3.5 boxes' on screen where an integer was expected.

steps.title: Operators
steps.body:
- `/` always gives a **double**: `7 / 2` is `3.5`.
- `~/` is integer division: `7 ~/ 2` is `3`.
- `%` is remainder: `7 % 2` is `1`.
- Strings: `'Hi $name'` and `'Total ${a + b}'` use interpolation. Triple quotes `'''` make multi-line strings.

steps.title: Trace it
steps.body:
```dart
int a = 17;
int b = 5;
print(a ~/ b);   // 3
print(a % b);    // 2
print(a / b);    // 3.4
print('a=$a, sum=${a + b}'); // a=17, sum=22
```

steps.title: Type facts
steps.body: `int` and `double` are both subtypes of `num`. `int x = 5.0;` is an error, while `double y = 5;` is allowed in current Dart because integer literals can be used where a double is expected.

steps.title: The null operators
steps.body:
- `String? name;` may be null; `String name2 = 'x';` never is.
- `name ?? 'guest'` gives a default if null.
- `name?.length` returns null instead of crashing if name is null.
- `name!` asserts non-null; it throws at runtime if wrong, so use it rarely.
- `late` promises you will initialise a non-nullable variable before use.

- Scattering `!` to silence the compiler: this moves the error to runtime.
- Marking fields `late` and forgetting to initialise them (LateInitializationError).

scenes.text: Zoya's app crashes with 'Unexpectedly found nil while unwrapping an Optional value'.
Somewhere a value was force-unwrapped with an exclamation mark.

steps.title: Core syntax
steps.body:
- `let` is a constant; `var` is mutable.
- An optional `String?` holds a String or nil.
- Safe unwrapping: `if let n = name { ... }`, `guard let n = name else { return }`, nil-coalescing `name ?? "guest"`.
- Force unwrap `name!` crashes if nil.

steps.title: Trace it
steps.body:
```swift
let name: String? = nil
print(name ?? "guest")      // guest
if let n = name { print(n) } // not executed
let len = name?.count        // nil (type Int?)
```

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using `!` because the compiler complained, which moves the error to runtime.
- Shadowing a variable name inside if let and being confused about which one is changed.
- Confusing `nil` with an empty string.

steps.title: Frame budget
steps.body: Frame time budget = 1000 ms divided by the refresh rate. At 60 Hz that is about 16.7 ms per frame; at 90 Hz about 11.1 ms; at 120 Hz about 8.3 ms. If the work for a frame (build, layout, paint, GPU raster) exceeds the budget, a frame is dropped: this is **jank**.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
1000 / 60 = 16.67 ms. 1000 / 120 = 8.33 ms.
A frame taking 12 ms is fine at 60 Hz but janky at 120 Hz.

steps.title: Profile in the right mode
steps.body: Measure performance in profile or release mode on a real device. Debug builds are much slower and misleading.

lessons.title: OSI and TCP/IP: the layered map

scenes.text: Ananya from HR says the intranet page 'does not load'. Her colleague says 'the network is down'. Dev, the junior engineer, asks one question: does the page fail for everyone, or only for her?
That question is a layer question. Cable, address, route, port, or application all fail differently, and a layered model is how engineers avoid guessing.

steps.title: Why layers exist
steps.body:
A **layer** hides complexity: each layer offers a service to the layer above and uses the service below. Changing Wi-Fi to fibre does not force a rewrite of your web browser.

- **Interoperability**: vendors implement the same layer interface.
- **Troubleshooting**: you can test one layer at a time.
- **Teaching**: a shared vocabulary ('that is a Layer 2 problem').

steps.title: The seven OSI layers (top to bottom)
steps.body:
7 **Application** - network services to apps (HTTP, DNS, SMTP)
6 **Presentation** - encoding, compression, encryption format (TLS is often placed here or at 5)
5 **Session** - starts, manages and ends dialogues
4 **Transport** - end-to-end delivery, ports, TCP/UDP
3 **Network** - logical addressing and routing (IP)
2 **Data Link** - framing, MAC addressing, local delivery (Ethernet, Wi-Fi)
1 **Physical** - bits as signals on copper, fibre or radio

steps.title: The TCP/IP model
steps.body: TCP/IP has four layers: **Application** (OSI 5-7), **Transport** (4), **Internet** (3) and **Network Access / Link** (1-2). Many textbooks also show a five-layer hybrid that splits Link into Data Link and Physical. The real protocols follow TCP/IP; OSI is the reference vocabulary.

steps.title: PDU names
steps.body: The **protocol data unit** is called *data* at the upper layers, **segment** (TCP) or **datagram** (UDP) at Layer 4, **packet** at Layer 3, **frame** at Layer 2 and **bits** at Layer 1.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying 'a router works at Layer 2'. Routers forward on Layer 3 but have Layer 2 interfaces too.
- Treating OSI as the protocol stack in use. The Internet runs TCP/IP.
- Mixing 'packet' and 'frame': a frame wraps a packet.

lessons.title: Lab: Encapsulation order for a web request

story.title: What happens when Ananya presses Enter

scenes.text: Ananya types https://intranet.contoso.local. Before anything leaves her laptop, each layer adds its own header, like nested envelopes.
Dev draws it on the whiteboard: data, segment, packet, frame, bits - and the reverse at the server.

steps.title: Encapsulation
steps.body: On the sender each layer adds a header (and the link layer a trailer): HTTP request -> **TCP segment** (source/destination port, sequence numbers) -> **IP packet** (source/destination IP) -> **Ethernet frame** (source/destination MAC, FCS trailer) -> bits on the wire.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Laptop 192.168.10.25 requests the server 10.20.0.80 port 443. Segment: src port 51514, dst 443. Packet: src 192.168.10.25, dst 10.20.0.80. Frame: dst MAC is the **default gateway** (not the server) because the server is on a different network.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: The destination MAC changes at every router hop; the destination **IP** stays the same end to end (ignoring NAT).

steps.title: Reading tcpdump-style lines
steps.body: A line such as `IP 192.168.10.25.51514 > 10.20.0.80.443: Flags [S]` shows Layer 3 addresses, a Layer 4 port after each address, and TCP flags. `[S]` = SYN, `[S.]` = SYN-ACK, `[.]` = ACK.

steps.title: Handshake
steps.body: 1. Client sends SYN. 2. Server replies SYN-ACK. 3. Client sends ACK. After that, data flows with `[P.]` (PSH-ACK).

steps.title: Tip
steps.body: Use `cat` to look at the file, then search for flags with grep. Always read a few lines in context first.

steps.body: An IPv4 address is **32 bits** written as four **octets** (8 bits each) separated by dots. Each octet ranges 0-255 because 2^8 = 256 values.

steps.title: The two formulas
steps.body: Usable hosts = **2^h - 2** (h = host bits; subtract network and broadcast addresses). Subnets created from a classful network = **2^s** where s = borrowed bits.

steps.title: MAC address
steps.body: A **MAC address** is 48 bits written as 6 hex pairs (e.g. 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E). The first 24 bits are the OUI (vendor); the rest identifies the interface. It is used only on the local segment.

steps.title: Ethernet frame
steps.body: Destination MAC (6) + Source MAC (6) + EtherType (2) + payload (46-1500) + FCS (4). The minimum frame is 64 bytes, the standard payload MTU is 1500.

steps.title: ARP
steps.body: **ARP** maps an IPv4 address to a MAC address on the same subnet: broadcast request (ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff), unicast reply. Replies are cached in the ARP table for minutes.

steps.title: Security note
steps.body: ARP has no authentication, so ARP spoofing is possible; switches can defend with Dynamic ARP Inspection.

steps.title: Mistake
steps.body: Thinking ARP crosses routers. It does not; you ARP for the gateway, never for a remote host.

steps.title: NAT
steps.body: **Network Address Translation** rewrites IP addresses (and with PAT, ports) as packets cross a border. It conserves public IPv4 addresses and hides internal addressing - but it is **not a firewall** and breaks end-to-end transparency.

steps.title: Terms
steps.body: **Inside local**: the inside host's private address. **Inside global**: how the inside host appears outside. **Outside global**: the outside host's real address. **Outside local**: how the outside host appears inside (usually the same as outside global).

steps.title: Types
steps.body: **Static NAT**: one-to-one fixed mapping (publish a server). **Dynamic NAT**: pool of public addresses, first come first served. **PAT / overload**: many inside hosts share one address distinguished by source port.

steps.title: Mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting `ip nat inside` / `ip nat outside` on interfaces.
- ACL for NAT that does not match the inside subnet.
- Treating NAT as security.

steps.title: ACL rules
steps.body: ACLs are processed **top-down, first match wins**; there is an **implicit deny any** at the end. Standard ACLs (1-99, 1300-1999) match source IP only; extended ACLs (100-199, 2000-2699) match protocol, source, destination and ports. Named ACLs allow editing by sequence numbers.

steps.title: Wildcard masks
steps.body: A **0 bit means must match**, **1 means ignore**. /24 -> 0.0.0.255; host -> 0.0.0.0 (or the `host` keyword); any -> 255.255.255.255 (`any`).

steps.title: Placement
steps.body: Put **extended** ACLs close to the **source** (stop unwanted traffic early); put **standard** ACLs close to the **destination** (they only see the source, so applying them near the source could block too much).

steps.title: Mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting `permit ip any any` before the implicit deny.
- Applying in the wrong direction.
- Wrong order: a broad permit above a specific deny.

steps.title: TCP
steps.body: Connection-oriented, reliable: three-way handshake, sequence/ack numbers, retransmission, flow control (window) and congestion control. Header minimum 20 bytes.

steps.title: UDP
steps.body: Connectionless, best effort, 8-byte header, no ordering or retransmission. Used by DNS queries, DHCP, NTP, VoIP/video, QUIC.

steps.title: Ports
steps.body: 22 SSH, 23 Telnet, 25 SMTP, 53 DNS, 67/68 DHCP, 80 HTTP, 110 POP3, 123 NTP, 143 IMAP, 161 SNMP, 443 HTTPS, 514 syslog (UDP), 3389 RDP. Well-known: 0-1023; registered: 1024-49151; dynamic: 49152-65535.

steps.title: Mistake
steps.body: Saying DNS only uses UDP. It uses UDP 53 normally and TCP 53 for large responses and zone transfers.

steps.title: Notation
steps.body: 128 bits as eight 16-bit hex groups separated by colons. Rule 1: drop leading zeros in a group. Rule 2: replace **one** run of consecutive all-zero groups with `::` (only once per address).

steps.title: Types
steps.body: Global unicast 2000::/3; link-local fe80::/10; unique local fc00::/7 (fd00::/8 used); multicast ff00::/8; loopback ::1; unspecified ::; documentation 2001:db8::/32. There are no broadcasts: multicast and anycast instead. Standard LAN prefix is /64.

steps.title: Mistake
steps.body: Using `::` twice, or shortening 2001:db8:0:0:1:0:0:1 incorrectly (only one run may be compressed; the longest run is preferred).

lessons.title: How a switch learns and forwards

scenes.text: On day one at Contoso's new floor, Dev plugs in a switch and wonders how it knows which cable leads to which PC.
Your turn: read the key ideas, then apply them hands-on in the activity that follows.

steps.title: Three jobs
steps.body: A Layer 2 switch **learns** the source MAC of every frame (recording MAC -> port in the CAM/MAC table), **forwards** known unicast out one port, and **floods** unknown unicast, broadcast and (by default) multicast out all other ports in the VLAN.

steps.title: Collision and broadcast domains
steps.body: Each switch port is its own collision domain (full duplex makes collisions irrelevant). All ports in one VLAN share a **broadcast domain**; routers (or Layer 3 switch interfaces) separate broadcast domains.

steps.title: Example
steps.body: PC-A (0050.7966.6800) on Fa0/1 sends to PC-B (unknown). The switch records 6800 on Fa0/1 and floods. When PC-B replies from Fa0/2 the switch learns that MAC too; later frames are unicast.

steps.title: Aging
steps.body: Dynamic MAC entries age out after 300 seconds by default on Cisco switches.

steps.title: Mistake
steps.body: Thinking a switch forwards by IP address. A Layer 2 switch only uses MAC addresses.

lessons.title: Loops, broadcast storms and the STP election

scenes.text: Someone plugs a patch cable between two wall ports on the same switch. Within seconds the floor goes dead: CPU 99%, link LEDs blinking in sync.
Your turn: read the key ideas, then apply them hands-on in the activity that follows.

steps.title: Why
steps.body: Ethernet frames have no TTL. A looped broadcast is copied forever -> **broadcast storm**, MAC table instability, multiple frame copies.

steps.title: STP
steps.body: Spanning Tree Protocol (802.1D) builds a loop-free tree: elect one **root bridge** (lowest Bridge ID = priority + MAC), each non-root picks one **root port** (lowest path cost to root), each segment gets one **designated port**; the rest are **blocking**.

steps.title: Bridge ID
steps.body: Priority (default 32768, in steps of 4096) + system-ID extension (VLAN ID) + MAC. VLAN 10 default priority = 32768 + 10 = 32778.

steps.title: Costs (short method)
steps.body: 10 Mbps = 100, 100 Mbps = 19, 1 Gbps = 4, 10 Gbps = 2. RSTP (802.1w) converges in a few seconds; PVST+/Rapid PVST+ run an instance per VLAN.

steps.title: Mistake
steps.body: Leaving the root to chance: the oldest switch (lowest MAC) may win. Set the root priority deliberately.

steps.title: Selection order
steps.body: 1) **Longest prefix match** wins first. 2) If the same prefix is learned from several sources, lowest **administrative distance (AD)** wins. 3) Within one protocol, lowest **metric** wins.

courses.summary: Link-state routing from first principles: LSAs, the neighbour state machine, DR/BDR, cost, router ID and single-area configuration - with simulated verification labs and verified cost/wildcard drills.
outcomes: Describe the OSPF neighbour states and DR/BDR election

scenes.text: Contoso now has 14 routers. Meera: 'Static routes don't scale, and they don't react when a link dies.'
Your turn: read the key ideas, then apply them hands-on in the activity that follows.

steps.title: Link-state
steps.body: Each router floods **LSAs** describing its links; all routers in an area build the same **LSDB** and run Dijkstra's SPF to compute shortest paths. Metric = **cost** = reference bandwidth / interface bandwidth (default reference 100 Mbps).

steps.title: Neighbour states
steps.body: Down -> Init -> 2-Way -> ExStart -> Exchange -> Loading -> **Full**. On broadcast networks a **DR** and **BDR** are elected (highest priority, then highest router ID; priority 0 = ineligible); other routers reach Full only with the DR/BDR and stay 2-Way with each other.

steps.title: Facts
steps.body: OSPF runs directly over IP protocol 89, multicast 224.0.0.5 (all OSPF routers) and 224.0.0.6 (DR/BDR). Hello/Dead timers: 10/40 s on broadcast and point-to-point.

steps.title: Neighbour must-match
steps.body: Area, hello/dead timers, subnet and mask, authentication, stub flag, and MTU (for adjacency to reach Full) - a unique router ID is also required.

steps.title: Wildcard
steps.body: Wildcard = inverse of the mask: /24 -> 0.0.0.255; /26 -> 0.0.0.63.

steps.title: FHRP
steps.body: A **First-Hop Redundancy Protocol** gives hosts one **virtual IP** (their default gateway) shared by two or more routers. One is **Active** (HSRP) / Master (VRRP) and answers ARP for the virtual IP using a virtual MAC; the other is Standby/Backup.

steps.title: HSRP details
steps.body: Cisco-proprietary, hello 3 s, hold 10 s by default; priority default 100, higher wins; **preempt** lets a higher-priority router take back the role. Virtual MAC for HSRPv1: 0000.0c07.acXX (XX = group). VRRP is the open standard (RFC 5798).

steps.title: Design
steps.body: Make DS1 Active for odd VLANs and DS2 Active for even VLANs to share load; track uplinks so a router with a dead uplink lowers its priority.

lessons.title: The method: scope, hypothesise, test, verify

scenes.text: At 9:05 four tickets arrive saying 'the network is slow'. Meera asks Dev for one sentence per ticket stating what is known, not guessed.

steps.title: Steps
steps.body: 1) Define the problem precisely (who, what, since when, what changed). 2) Gather facts (logs, show commands, tests). 3) Form hypotheses ranked by likelihood and cost to test. 4) Test one change at a time. 5) Implement the fix. 6) Verify with the user. 7) Document root cause and fix.

steps.title: Approaches
steps.body: **Bottom-up** (start at Layer 1), **top-down** (start at the application), **divide and conquer** (start mid-stack, e.g. ping, then move up or down), **follow the path** (trace the packet's route), **compare working vs non-working**, **swap the component**.

steps.title: Mistakes
steps.body:
- Changing several things at once.
- Not recording the original config.
- Closing the ticket without user confirmation.
- Skipping 'what changed?'

courses.summary: A gentle first step into coding for children: algorithms, sequences, loops, conditions and debugging, practised with the turtle-drawing lab and the code maze game.
outcomes: Learners can write a clear step-by-step algorithm for an everyday task
Learners can spot repeated steps and replace them with a loop
Learners can use if/else to make a program choose
Learners can find and fix a bug by testing one step at a time

story.title: Anaya makes lemonade for a robot

scenes.text: Anaya in Pune wanted her toy robot Chotu to make lemonade. She said: 'Make lemonade!' Chotu did nothing.
Her brother Kabir laughed: 'Chotu only understands tiny, exact steps. You must tell it EVERYTHING, in the right order.'
Anaya wrote: 1. Take a glass. 2. Squeeze half a lemon into it. 3. Add 2 spoons of sugar. 4. Pour water. 5. Stir 10 times.
When they acted it out, Kabir poured water before taking the glass — splash! Order matters. Anaya had just written her first algorithm.

steps.title: What is an algorithm?
steps.body:
An **algorithm** is a list of steps that solves a problem, written so clearly that anyone (or any machine) following it gets the same result.

You already use algorithms every day:
- brushing your teeth
- tying your shoelaces
- the way you walk to school

A **program** is just an algorithm written in a language a computer understands, such as Python, JavaScript or Scratch blocks.

steps.title: Three rules of a good algorithm
steps.body:
- **Exact:** 'add some sugar' is unclear; 'add 2 spoons of sugar' is exact.
- **In order:** the steps happen one after another, top to bottom. This is called a **sequence**.
- **Finishes:** it must stop. 'Keep stirring' with no end would go on forever.

Computers are very fast but not clever: they do exactly what you say, not what you mean.

steps.title: Worked example: drawing a square
steps.body:
Imagine a turtle on paper holding a pen. It understands only: *forward(steps)* and *turn right(degrees)*.

To draw a square:
- forward 100, right 90
- forward 100, right 90
- forward 100, right 90
- forward 100, right 90

Why 90? A square has 4 corners and the turtle must turn all the way round (360 degrees) by the end: 360 ÷ 4 = 90.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- **Skipping a step** because it feels obvious to you ('take a glass'). The computer does not know it.
- **Wrong order** — pouring before holding the glass.
- **Vague words** like 'a little', 'nicely', 'soon'. Replace them with numbers.

steps.title: Try this (unplugged)
steps.body: Ask a grown-up or friend to be the 'robot'. Write steps to make them walk from the door to a chair. They must follow your words *exactly* — no guessing! Every time they bump into something, fix your algorithm. Then open the **turtle lab** and draw a square with the 8 steps above.

activity.prompt: Put Anaya's lemonade algorithm in the right order.
items: Take a clean glass
Squeeze half a lemon into the glass
Add 2 spoons of sugar
Pour water until the glass is nearly full
Stir 10 times
Serve the lemonade

options: A clear list of steps that solves a problem
quiz.why: An algorithm is a precise, ordered set of steps. Programs are algorithms written for computers.
A number makes an instruction exact, so everyone gets the same result. 'Some' or 'soon' can mean different things to different people.

quiz.q: To draw a square, the turtle turns right by how many degrees at each corner?
quiz.why: A square has 4 equal corners, and the turtle must turn a full 360 degrees in total. So each turn is 360 ÷ 4 = 90 degrees.

quiz.q: Steps that happen one after another in order are called a…
quiz.why: Steps done one after another in order are a sequence. It is the most basic idea in coding.

quiz.q: Why did Chotu do nothing when told 'Make lemonade!'?
quiz.why: Computers cannot fill gaps. Big vague commands must be broken into small exact steps.

lessons.title: Loops: say it once, repeat it many times

scenes.text: Rohan in Chennai wrote the square steps for his turtle: forward, right, forward, right… eight lines.
Then his teacher Ms. Fernandes asked for a star with 5 points, then a shape with 36 sides. 'That is 72 lines!' Rohan groaned.
Ms. Fernandes smiled: 'When you see the same steps again and again, use a loop. Repeat 4 times: forward 100, right 90.'
Rohan's 36-sided shape took just 3 lines. It looked almost like a circle.

steps.title: What is a loop?
steps.body:
A **loop** repeats a group of steps. Instead of writing the same thing many times, you write it once and say how many times to repeat.

In block languages: *repeat 4 [ forward 100, right 90 ]*.
In Python it looks like this:
for i in range(4):
    forward(100)
    right(90)

The indented lines (pushed in with spaces) are the **body** of the loop — the part that repeats.

steps.title: Worked example: any regular shape
steps.body:
For a shape with **n** equal sides, the turtle turns 360 ÷ n degrees at each corner.
- Triangle: repeat 3 [forward 100, right 120]
- Pentagon: repeat 5 [forward 100, right 72]
- Hexagon: repeat 6 [forward 100, right 60]
- 36 sides: repeat 36 [forward 10, right 10] — looks like a circle.

A 5-pointed star is different: repeat 5 [forward 100, right 144]. The turtle goes round **twice** (5 × 144 = 720).

steps.title: Loops are everywhere
steps.body: A washing machine repeats spin cycles. A music app repeats a song. A traffic light repeats green-yellow-red all day. Computers can repeat millions of times per second without getting bored — that is their superpower.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Putting a step **inside** the loop that should be **outside** (for example, 'pen up' inside the loop stops the drawing).
- Wrong turn angle — check that turns add up to 360 (or 720 for a star).
- A loop that never stops is called an **infinite loop**. Always know when your loop should end.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: In the turtle lab: draw a triangle, a hexagon and a star using loops. Challenge: put a loop **inside** a loop — repeat 12 [ draw a square, right 30 ] — and see the flower pattern appear.

activity.prompt: Match each shape to the loop that draws it.

options: To repeat steps without rewriting them
quiz.why: Loops save writing and make code easier to change: edit once, every repeat changes.

quiz.q: A turtle turns right 72 degrees, 5 times. What shape?
quiz.why: A turn of 72 degrees, 5 times, makes 72 × 5 = 360 degrees. A shape with 5 equal sides is a pentagon.

options: A loop that runs exactly once
quiz.why: If nothing ever tells the loop to stop, it runs forever and the program freezes.

quiz.q: In Python, how do we show which lines are inside a loop?
options: Put them in a different file
quiz.why: Python uses indentation, usually 4 spaces, to show which lines are inside the loop.

quiz.q: Turn angle for a regular shape with 8 sides?
quiz.why: The turn angle is 360 divided by the number of sides. For 8 sides, 360 ÷ 8 = 45 degrees.

lessons.title: If this, then that: making choices

scenes.text: Meher in Kochi built a tiny program for her school project: a robot that reminds people what to carry.
'If it is raining, say: take an umbrella. Otherwise, say: take sunglasses.'
Her friend Arjun tested it: rain → umbrella. Sun → sunglasses. Then he asked: 'What if it is very cold?' Meher added another choice.
Her robot now made decisions. 'That,' said her teacher, 'is the difference between a list of steps and a smart program.'

steps.title: Conditions
steps.body:
A **condition** is a question with a yes/no (true/false) answer: *Is it raining? Is the score more than 10? Is there a wall ahead?*

An **if** statement runs some steps only when the condition is true. An **else** gives the steps for when it is false.

In Python:
if raining:
    print('Take an umbrella')
else:
    print('Take sunglasses')

steps.title: Worked example: more than two choices
Choices in real machines
steps.body:
- A lift: if a button is pressed on floor 3, go to floor 3.
- A game: if the player touches a coin, add 1 point.
- A phone: if the battery is below 20%, show a warning.
- The code maze: if there is a wall ahead, turn; else move forward.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Checking in the wrong order: if you test 'temperature < 25' first, a cold day (8) also matches and you never reach the sweater advice.
- Forgetting the **else** case — what should happen when nothing matches?
- Mixing up **=** (store a value) and **==** (compare two values) in Python.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Play the **code maze** game. Before each move, say your condition aloud: 'If there is a wall in front, I turn right; otherwise I go forward.' Count how many moves your rule needs to escape.

a.text: Your maze robot sees a wall straight ahead and an open path on the right. Which rule should it follow?

choices.label: If wall ahead → turn right
choices.feedback: Yes! A condition checks the wall before moving.

choices.label: Always move forward
choices.feedback: Without a condition, the robot crashes into the wall.

b.text: Now the path ahead is open. What should the robot do?

choices.label: Else → move forward
choices.feedback: Right — the else branch handles the open path.

choices.label: Turn right again
choices.feedback: Turning when the path is open wastes moves and can send you in circles.

c.text: Bonk! The robot bumped the wall or spun in a circle. Bugs like this are normal — let's try again with a condition.

choices.label: Try again
choices.feedback: Good — coders learn by testing and fixing.

d.text: The robot escapes the maze using one simple rule: if wall ahead, turn right; else move forward. You wrote a decision-making program!

options: Runs steps only when a condition is true
quiz.why: An 'if' statement runs its steps only when a condition is true. If it is false, those steps are skipped.

quiz.q: A condition always has an answer of…
quiz.why: A condition is a yes/no question, so its answer is always True or False. These are called Boolean values.

quiz.q: temperature = 30. Using Meher's code, what prints?
quiz.why: 30 is not less than 10, and not less than 25, so the else part runs. It prints 'Drink lots of water!'.

quiz.q: In Python, which symbol compares two values?
quiz.why: The symbol == compares two values and asks 'are they equal?'. A single = stores a value in a variable.
'else' is the 'otherwise' part. It runs when the condition is false.

lessons.title: Bugs and debugging: be a code detective

scenes.text: Kabir wanted his turtle to draw a house: a square with a triangle roof. He got a square… and a roof floating in the sky.
He wanted to delete everything and start again. His grandmother, a retired engineer in Bengaluru, said: 'Wait. Let's be detectives.'
They ran the program one step at a time and watched where the turtle went. After the square, the turtle was facing the wrong way.
One extra 'right 90' fixed it. 'Every programmer in the world has bugs,' said Nani. 'Good programmers find them calmly.'

steps.title: What is a bug?
steps.body:
A **bug** is a mistake in a program that makes it do something you did not want. Fixing it is called **debugging**.

There are three common kinds:
- **Syntax error:** the computer cannot understand the code (a missing bracket, a spelling mistake like 'pirnt').
- **Runtime error:** the program starts but crashes (for example, dividing by zero).
- **Logic error:** the program runs but gives the wrong answer — like Kabir's floating roof. These are the trickiest.

steps.title: The detective method
steps.body:
- **Reproduce:** run it again — does the bug happen every time?
- **Predict:** say what *should* happen at each step.
- **Observe:** run one step at a time, or add print() lines to see values.
- **Find the first surprise:** the bug is near the first step where reality differs from your prediction.
- **Fix one thing, then test again.**

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Goal: add up 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 15.
total = 0
for n in range(5):
    total = total + n
print(total)

This prints **10**, not 15. Detective work: print n inside the loop → we see 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. range(5) starts at 0 and stops *before* 5! Fix: range(1, 6). Now it prints 15.

steps.title: Rubber duck debugging
steps.body: Explain your code, line by line, out loud to a rubber duck (or a toy, or a pet). Saying it slowly often makes you notice the mistake yourself. Professional programmers really do this.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: In the turtle lab, deliberately add one wrong turn to your square and watch what happens. Then fix it. Breaking things on purpose is a great way to understand them.

activity.prompt: Sort each bug into its type.

The roof drawn in the wrong place

options: Finding and fixing mistakes in code
quiz.why: Debugging means finding and fixing mistakes (bugs) in code.

quiz.q: The program runs but gives the wrong answer. This is a…
quiz.why: A program that runs but gives the wrong answer has a logic error. It doesn't crash, so the mistake is easy to miss.

quiz.q: What does range(5) give in Python?
quiz.why: range(5) starts at 0 and stops just before 5, so it gives 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. That is five numbers.

quiz.q: Best first step when you find a bug?
options: Reproduce it and predict each step
quiz.why: First reproduce the bug and predict what each step should do. Then watch what really happens, and fix one thing at a time.

quiz.q: Why explain code to a rubber duck?
options: Explaining slowly helps you spot your own mistake
quiz.why: Explaining your code slowly, step by step, helps you notice the part that does not make sense. The duck does not need to know Python.

options: A clear ordered list of steps
questions.why: An algorithm is a clear, ordered list of steps to do a job.

options: if it rains, take an umbrella

The word 'else' means 'otherwise'. It runs when the 'if' condition is false.

questions.why: A program that starts fine and then fails while running, like when dividing by zero, has a runtime error. A syntax error would stop it from starting.

questions.q: for i in range(3): print('Hi') prints Hi how many times?
questions.why: range(3) gives 0, 1, 2, which is three values. So the loop runs 3 times and prints Hi three times.

questions.q: x = 7. if x > 5: print('big') else: print('small'). Output?
questions.why: x is 7, and 7 > 5 is True, so the if part runs and prints 'big'.

questions.why: The detective method is: reproduce the bug, predict what should happen, observe what does happen, then fix one thing.
Turning 144 degrees 5 times gives 720 degrees, which is two full turns. The turtle goes round twice and draws a five-point star.

questions.why: The loop adds 1, then 2, then 3 to total: 1 + 2 + 3 = 6. range(1,4) stops before 4.

questions.why: 10 is not less than 10, so the first rule fails. 10 is less than 25, so the second rule runs and gives T-shirt.

questions.q: repeat 12 [draw a square, right 30] — how far has the turtle turned in total from the 'right 30' steps?
questions.why: Each 'right 30' turns 30 degrees, and 12 × 30 = 360. That's one full turn, which makes a symmetrical flower pattern.

courses.title: Python from zero
courses.summary: Learn real Python from absolute zero: values and variables, decisions and loops, functions, lists and dictionaries, and handling errors — with worked examples you can type and run.
outcomes: Learners can store and convert data with variables and types
Learners can write programs that decide and repeat
Learners can design reusable functions with parameters and return values
Learners can organise data in lists and dictionaries
Learners can read errors, handle exceptions and build a small project

scenes.text: Priya runs a chai stall outside a Hyderabad metro station. Each evening she adds up cups sold on a paper slip — and often gets it wrong when tired.
Her nephew Sameer, a Class 10 student, said: 'Let's make Python do the maths.' He typed: cups = 140 and price = 15.
Then: total = cups * price, and print(total). The screen showed 2100. Priya laughed: 'So the computer just remembers numbers in named boxes?'
'Exactly,' said Sameer. 'Those boxes are called variables.'

steps.title: Your first program
steps.body:
Python runs your file from top to bottom, one line at a time.
print('Namaste, world!')

**print()** shows something on screen. The text inside quotes is a **string** (a piece of text). You can use single or double quotes, but they must match.

To run Python you can install it from python.org and use IDLE, or use any free online Python editor. Type each example yourself — typing builds memory far better than reading.

steps.title: Variables
steps.body:
A **variable** is a name that refers to a value.
cups = 140
price = 15
total = cups * price
print(total)   # 2100

- The **=** sign means *store the right side under the name on the left* — it is not maths equality.
- Names may use letters, digits and underscores, cannot start with a digit, and are case-sensitive (Total and total are different).
- Choose meaningful names: cups_sold beats x.
- Anything after # is a **comment** for humans; Python ignores it.

steps.title: The four basic types
steps.body:
- **int** — whole numbers: 140, -3
- **float** — decimals: 15.5, 0.1
- **str** — text: 'chai', '140'
- **bool** — True or False

Use type(x) to check. Arithmetic: + - * / (always gives a float: 7 / 2 = 3.5), // (floor division: 7 // 2 = 3), % (remainder: 7 % 2 = 1), ** (power: 2 ** 3 = 8).

steps.title: Worked example: input and conversion
steps.body:
input() always returns a **string**, even if the user types a number.
cups = input('Cups sold? ')      # user types 140 → '140'
price = 15
print(cups * price)               # surprise!

'140' * 15 repeats the text 15 times! Convert first:
cups = int(input('Cups sold? '))
print(cups * price)               # 2100

To combine text and numbers neatly, use an **f-string**:
print(f'Today: {cups} cups, Rs {cups * price}')

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting int() or float() around input().
- 'Total: ' + 2100 → TypeError (cannot add str and int). Use an f-string or str(2100).
- Using a variable before giving it a value → NameError.
- Expecting 0.1 + 0.2 to be exactly 0.3 — floats are stored in binary, so you get 0.30000000000000004. For money, round(x, 2) when displaying, or count in paise as integers.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write a program that asks for a temperature in Celsius and prints it in Fahrenheit. Formula: F = C × 9 / 5 + 32. Test with 100 (should print 212.0) and 37 (about 98.6 — round() tidies tiny float errors).

activity.prompt: Fill in the Python so the program works.

quiz.why: A single = is assignment: it stores 140 under the name cups. To compare values you use ==.

quiz.q: Type of the value returned by input()?
quiz.why: input() always returns text (a str). To do maths on it you must convert it with int() or float().
17 // 5 is floor division, so 3 (5 × 3 = 15). 17 % 5 is the remainder, 17 − 15 = 2.

quiz.q: Which variable name is NOT allowed?
quiz.why: Variable names cannot start with a digit, so 2nd_day is not allowed. Letters, digits and underscores are fine if the name doesn't start with a digit.
With strings, + joins (concatenates) the text. So '5' + '5' is '55', not 10.

scenes.text: Fatima teaches Class 9 in Lucknow. Every term she converts 40 students' marks into grades by hand.
Her former student Dev, now in college, offered: 'A loop can go through every mark, and if/elif can choose the grade.'
In fifteen lines they had a program that printed every grade and the class average.
Fatima used the saved hour to plan a better lesson.

steps.title: Comparisons and logic
for loops
steps.body:
A **for** loop takes each item from a sequence in turn.
marks = [88, 92, 45, 30]
for m in marks:
    print(m)

**range()** produces numbers: range(5) → 0..4; range(1, 11) → 1..10; range(0, 20, 5) → 0, 5, 10, 15.

steps.title: while loops, break and continue
steps.body:
A **while** loop repeats as long as a condition is True — useful when you do not know the count in advance.
pin = ''
while pin != '4321':
    pin = input('PIN: ')
print('Welcome')

- **break** leaves the loop immediately.
- **continue** skips to the next repetition.
Always make sure something inside the loop eventually makes the condition False.

steps.title: Worked example: class average and topper
steps.body:
marks = [88, 92, 45, 30, 76]
total = 0
best = marks[0]
for m in marks:
    total += m           # same as total = total + m
    if m > best:
        best = m
avg = total / len(marks)
print(f'Average {avg:.1f}, highest {best}')

Output: Average 66.2, highest 92. (Python also has sum(marks) and max(marks), but writing it yourself teaches the **accumulator pattern** used everywhere.)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Order of elif matters: test the highest range first, or 95 might be graded 'Pass'.
- **Off-by-one:** range(1, 10) stops at 9.
- Infinite while loop: forgetting to update the variable the condition depends on.
- Using = instead of == inside if → SyntaxError.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: FizzBuzz, a classic interview warm-up: print numbers 1 to 30, but print 'Fizz' for multiples of 3, 'Buzz' for multiples of 5, and 'FizzBuzz' for multiples of both. Hint: check the 'both' case (n % 15 == 0) first.

statements.s: range(1, 5) produces 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.
statements.why: range stops before the end value: 1, 2, 3, 4.

statements.s: A while loop may run zero times.
statements.why: If the condition is False at the start, the body never runs.

statements.s: break skips only the current repetition.
statements.why: That is continue; break exits the whole loop.

statements.s: In if/elif/else, more than one branch can run.
statements.why: Only the first true branch runs.

statements.s: not (5 > 3) is False.
statements.why: 5 > 3 is True; not True is False.

quiz.q: marks = 80. With the grading code (>=90 A1, >=75 A2, >=33 Pass), the grade is…
quiz.why: 80 is not >= 90, so the first test fails. It passes >= 75, so the grade is A2.

quiz.q: How many numbers does range(0, 20, 5) produce?
quiz.why: range(0, 20, 5) starts at 0 and steps by 5 until before 20: 0, 5, 10, 15. That is 4 numbers.

quiz.q: Which loop is best when you do not know how many times to repeat?
quiz.why: A while loop repeats until a condition changes, so it fits when you don't know the number of repeats. A for loop with range needs a known count.

quiz.q: For FizzBuzz, why check n % 15 == 0 first?
options: Otherwise multiples of 15 would match the 3-check first and print only Fizz
quiz.why: A multiple of 15 is also a multiple of 3. If you check 3 first, it matches and prints only Fizz. Check the specific case (15) first.
total += m is shorthand for total = total + m. It adds m to the existing value.

lessons.title: Functions: name a job, reuse it

scenes.text: Arjun runs a small electronics shop in Jaipur. He kept copying the same three lines to add GST to every bill.
When he changed the formula, he forgot one copy — and undercharged a customer for a week.
His friend Neha, a developer, rewrote it as one function: add_tax(amount, rate). Every bill now called the same function.
'Change it in one place, fixed everywhere,' Neha said. 'That's the point of functions.'

steps.title: Defining and calling a function
steps.body:
A **function** is a named, reusable block of code.
def add_tax(amount, rate):
    tax = amount * rate / 100
    return amount + tax

bill = add_tax(1000, 18)
print(bill)   # 1180.0

- **def** starts the definition; amount and rate are **parameters**.
- 1000 and 18 are **arguments** — the actual values passed in.
- **return** sends a value back to the caller and ends the function.

steps.title: Defaults, keywords and scope
Worked example: break a problem into functions
print vs return — the #1 beginner confusion
steps.body:
def double(x):
    print(x * 2)
result = double(5)    # shows 10
print(result)         # None!

print only *shows* a value; return *gives it back* so other code can use it. A function without return gives back **None**. Also: writing double instead of double(5) refers to the function itself without running it.

steps.title: Good function habits
steps.body:
- Name functions with verbs: calculate_total, send_email.
- Keep them short (often under 20 lines).
- Write a docstring (a triple-quoted sentence) as the first line, saying what the function returns.
- Test with simple known answers first (100 at 18% → 118).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write bmi(weight_kg, height_m) that returns weight ÷ height². Then write category(b) returning 'under' if b < 18.5, 'normal' if b < 25, else 'over'. (These are the general WHO adult cut-offs; BMI is a rough screening number, not a diagnosis.)

activity.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Name in the definition that receives a value
Sends a result back to the caller
What a function gives back with no return

quiz.q: def f(x): return x + 1. What is f(f(2))?
A function with no return statement returns…
quiz.why: A function with no return statement returns None by default.

quiz.q: Is 1900 a leap year by the Gregorian rule?
quiz.why: 1900 is divisible by 100 but not by 400, so it is not a leap year in the Gregorian rule.

options: Reuse and change logic in one place
quiz.why: Functions let you reuse code and change the logic in one place. Arjun's bug came from code that was copied in several places.

quiz.q: add_tax(500, rate=5) with def add_tax(amount, rate=18) returns about…
quiz.why: With rate = 5, the function adds 5% tax: 500 × 1.05 = 525. The default of 18 is used only if no rate is given.

scenes.text: Grace volunteers at a community library in Shillong. The book register is a tattered notebook.
Her cousin Tenzin showed her a Python list for the shelf of titles, and a dictionary linking each title to who borrowed it.
Finding who had 'Wings of Fire' became one line: borrowed['Wings of Fire'].
Grace said: 'Lists are like a queue; dictionaries are like a phone book.' Tenzin grinned: 'Perfect description.'

steps.title: Lists: ordered collections
steps.body:
books = ['Malgudi Days', 'Wings of Fire', 'Gitanjali']
- Index from 0: books[0] is 'Malgudi Days'; books[-1] is the last item.
- books.append('Godaan') adds to the end; books.remove('Gitanjali') removes by value; len(books) counts.
- **Slicing:** books[0:2] gives the first two items.
- Lists are **mutable** — you can change them: books[1] = 'Ignited Minds'.
- 'Godaan' in books → True or False.

steps.title: Dictionaries: key → value
steps.body:
borrowed = {'Wings of Fire': 'Tenzin', 'Godaan': 'Ri'}
borrowed['Gitanjali'] = 'Grace'    # add or update
print(borrowed['Godaan'])          # Ri
print(borrowed.get('Malgudi Days', 'on shelf'))  # safe lookup
for title, person in borrowed.items():
    print(title, '→', person)

Keys must be unique and immutable (strings, numbers, tuples). Looking up a key in a dictionary is very fast, even with millions of entries.

steps.title: Worked example: counting words
Also useful: tuples, sets, comprehensions
steps.body:
- **tuple:** ('Pune', 18.5) — like a list but cannot be changed; good for fixed records.
- **set:** {'red', 'blue'} — unique items, no order; great for removing duplicates: set(names).
- **List comprehension:** squares = [n * n for n in range(1, 6)] → [1, 4, 9, 16, 25]. With a filter: [n for n in nums if n % 2 == 0].

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- books[3] on a 3-item list → IndexError (indexes are 0, 1, 2).
- borrowed['Unknown'] → KeyError; use .get() when the key might be missing.
- b = books does NOT copy — both names point to the same list. Use books.copy().
- Changing a list while looping over it causes skipped items; loop over a copy.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Make a dictionary of 5 friends' names → birth months. Write code that prints everyone born in a month you ask for with input(). Then use a set to print the distinct months.

activity.prompt: Which data structure fits best?

items.text: Songs in a playlist, in play order

quiz.why: A negative index counts from the end of the list. nums[-1] is the last item, 30.

quiz.q: Safe dictionary lookup that avoids KeyError?
quiz.why: d.get(k, default) returns the default value if the key is missing. d[k] raises a KeyError instead.
range(3) gives 0, 1, 2 and each is doubled: [0, 2, 4].
A set keeps only unique items. ['a', 'b', 'a', 'c'] has three different values, so len is 3.

quiz.q: b = books; b.append('X'). What happens to books?
quiz.why: b = books does not copy the list. Both names refer to the same list object, so appending through b also changes books.

lessons.title: Errors, exceptions and a mini project

scenes.text: Ravi, a first-year B.Com student in Kolkata, wanted to track his monthly spending on food, travel and mobile recharge.
His first version crashed whenever he typed 'fifty' instead of 50: ValueError: invalid literal for int().
He learned try/except, so the program politely asked again instead of crashing, and saved data to a file so nothing was lost overnight.
At month-end it printed totals by category. He discovered he spent more on snacks than on books.

steps.title: Reading a traceback
steps.body:
When Python crashes it prints a **traceback**. Read it from the **bottom**:
ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'fifty'
- The last line names the **error type** and message.
- Lines above show the file, line number and code that failed.
Common types: SyntaxError, NameError (unknown name), TypeError (wrong type), ValueError (right type, bad value), IndexError, KeyError, ZeroDivisionError, FileNotFoundError.

steps.title: try / except
Files
steps.body:
with open('expenses.csv', 'a', encoding='utf-8') as f:
    f.write(f'{category},{amount}\n')

- Modes: 'r' read, 'w' write (erases!), 'a' append.
- **with** closes the file automatically, even after an error.
- Reading: for line in open('expenses.csv', encoding='utf-8'): cat, amt = line.strip().split(',')

steps.title: Worked example: totals by category
Project habits that professionals use
steps.body:
- Start tiny: make one feature work, then add the next.
- Keep data separate from code (the CSV file).
- Test strange input: empty lines, negative numbers, text.
- Use **virtual environments** (python -m venv .venv) when you start installing packages with pip, so projects do not clash.
- Put your project under Git (see the Git lesson).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Build Ravi's tracker: a menu loop with options 1) add expense 2) show totals 3) quit. Handle bad input with try/except. Bonus: warn when any category passes a budget you set in a dictionary.

activity.prompt: Order the steps for adding one expense safely.
items: Show the menu and read the choice
Ask for the category
Ask for the amount inside try
If ValueError, explain and ask again
Open the file in append mode with 'with'
Write 'category,amount' and a newline
Confirm 'Saved' to the user

quiz.q: Where do you start reading a traceback?
quiz.why: Read a traceback from the bottom. The last line states the actual error and its message.
int('fifty') gets a string, which is the right type, but its value can't be converted to a number. That raises a ValueError.

quiz.q: Which file mode erases existing content?
quiz.why: Mode 'w' truncates (erases) the file before writing. Use 'a' to add to the end instead.
The 'with' statement closes the file automatically, even if an error happens in the block.
A bare 'except:' catches every error, including unexpected ones, which hides real bugs. Catch the specific errors you expect.

questions.why: 3.0 has a decimal point, so its type is float.
Python comments start with #. The other symbols are used in other languages.
In Python 3, / is true division and always returns a float, so 10 / 4 is 2.5.
def is the keyword for defining a function: def name(params):.
append adds one item at the end, so the list [1, 2, 3, 4] has length 4.

questions.q: for i in range(2, 10, 3): print(i) prints…
questions.why: range(2, 10, 3) starts at 2 and steps by 3, stopping before 10: 2, 5, 8.
d.get('b', 0) returns the default 0 because the key 'b' is missing. It doesn't raise a KeyError.

questions.q: A function prints a value but has no return. Its call evaluates to…
questions.why: Printing is not returning. A function with no return statement evaluates to None.
Strings are indexed from 0, so 'abc'[1] is the second letter, 'b'.

questions.q: What does [w.upper() for w in ['hi', 'yo'] if 'h' in w] produce?
questions.why: The loop only takes words that contain 'h'. Only 'hi' does, and it is made uppercase, giving ['HI'].
b = a doesn't copy the list. a and b are the same object, so appending to b changes a: [1, 2, 3].
Reading a missing key from a dictionary raises a KeyError.

questions.q: def f(n): return 1 if n <= 1 else n * f(n - 1). f(5)?
questions.why: The function is the recursive factorial: f(5) = 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 120.

options: Binary floating point cannot represent these decimals exactly
questions.why: Floats are binary approximations; compare with a tolerance (math.isclose) or use the decimal module.
The lambda sorts the (key, value) pairs by value, from smallest to largest. So ('b', 1) comes before ('a', 3).

courses.title: JavaScript from zero: make web pages come alive
courses.summary: Learn the language of the web: values and variables, functions, arrays and objects, the DOM and events, and asynchronous code with fetch — using only a browser.
outcomes: Learners can declare variables with let and const and explain JavaScript's types and equality
Learners can write functions, including arrow functions, and use array methods
Learners can change a web page in response to user events
Learners can fetch JSON data asynchronously and handle errors

lessons.title: Hello, browser: values, let and const

scenes.text: Zoya, a Class 11 student in Bhopal, wanted a web page showing how many days remain until her best friend Ishita's birthday.
She learned that every browser already contains a JavaScript engine. No installation needed: press F12, open the Console, and type.
Her first line: const today = new Date(); Her second: console.log(today). The date appeared. She was programming.

steps.title: Where JavaScript runs
steps.body:
JavaScript (JS) runs in every web browser and also on servers (Node.js). To start:
- Open any browser, press F12 (or right-click → Inspect) and choose **Console**.
- Type console.log('Namaste'); and press Enter.

In a web page, put code in a file app.js and load it from HTML with a script tag: <script src='app.js' defer></script>. The defer attribute runs it after the page is built.

steps.title: let, const (and why not var)
steps.body:
const name = 'Zoya';   // cannot be reassigned
let age = 16;           // can change
age = 17;

- Prefer **const**; use **let** only when the value must change.
- **var** is the old way: it ignores block scope and causes surprises. Modern code avoids it.
- Statements usually end with ; (optional in many cases, but be consistent).

steps.title: Types
steps.body:
- **number** (one type for whole and decimal: 42, 3.14)
- **string** ('hi', "hi", or a template literal in backticks: `Hi ${name}`)
- **boolean** (true/false)
- **undefined** (declared but no value), **null** (intentionally empty)
- **object** (including arrays and functions)
- also bigint and symbol (advanced)
Check with typeof: typeof 42 → 'number'.

steps.title: == vs === (always use ===)
steps.body:
== converts types before comparing, which gives strange results:
'5' == 5    // true
0 == ''     // true
'5' === 5   // false

**=== checks value AND type.** Use it every time. Similarly, '5' + 1 gives '51' (string joining) while '5' - 1 gives 4. Convert explicitly: Number('5').

steps.title: Worked example: days until a birthday
Try this
steps.body: In the console: make const price = 499 and let qty = 3. Log a template string like `Total: Rs ${price * qty}`. Then test '7' + 3, '7' - 3 and '7' === 7 and explain each result to yourself.

statements.s: '5' === 5 is true.
statements.why: === also compares type; a string is not a number.

statements.s: A const variable can be reassigned later.
statements.why: const prevents reassignment (though an object's contents can still change).

statements.s: new Date(2025, 0, 1) is 1 January 2025.
'10' - 2 evaluates to 8.
statements.why: The minus operator converts the string to a number.

statements.s: typeof null returns 'null'.
statements.why: A long-standing quirk: typeof null is 'object'.

quiz.q: Which keyword should you use by default for a variable?
quiz.why: Use const by default and only use let when you need to reassign the variable. This avoids accidental changes.
With a string on one side, + concatenates, so '3' + 4 is the string '34'. It doesn't add the numbers.
Template strings use backticks (`), which allow ${ } to put values inside text.

quiz.q: Where can you quickly try JS without installing anything?
quiz.why: Every modern browser has a developer console (open it with F12), where you can try JavaScript without installing anything.

quiz.q: What does the defer attribute on a script tag do?
options: Runs it after the HTML is parsed
quiz.why: The defer attribute makes the browser download the script while parsing and run it after the HTML is parsed. It doesn't block the page.

scenes.text: Kiran coaches an under-14 cricket team in Indore and keeps each player's runs in a spreadsheet.
He wanted a little web tool that showed each player's average and the top scorer.
His developer friend Laila said: 'Store each player as an object, put them in an array, and let array methods like map, filter and reduce do the work.'

steps.title: Functions three ways
Arrays
steps.body:
const runs = [45, 12, 78, 0, 33];
runs[0];          // 45
runs.length;      // 5
runs.push(50);    // add to end
runs.includes(78) // true

**Array methods take a function:**
- map → transform each item: runs.map(r => r * 2)
- filter → keep items that pass: runs.filter(r => r >= 30)
- reduce → combine into one value: runs.reduce((sum, r) => sum + r, 0)
- find, some, every, sort, forEach

steps.title: Objects and JSON
steps.body:
const player = { name: 'Aman', innings: [45, 12, 78], keeper: false };
player.name           // 'Aman'
player['keeper']      // false
player.age = 13;      // add a property
const { name, innings } = player;   // destructuring

**JSON** (JavaScript Object Notation) is the text format of objects used across the web: JSON.stringify(obj) → text, JSON.parse(text) → object. In JSON, keys must use double quotes.

steps.title: Worked example: averages and top scorer
Common mistakes
steps.body:
- [10, 9, 1].sort() gives [1, 10, 9] — sort compares as **text** by default. Use sort((a, b) => a - b).
- Forgetting reduce's starting value (0) on an empty array throws an error.
- An arrow function returning an object needs brackets: p => ({ ...p }).
- const arr = []; arr.push(1) is allowed — const stops reassignment, not mutation.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Using the team array: list the names of players with any century (some(r => r >= 100)), and the total runs of the whole team using map and reduce together.

activity.prompt: Match the array method to what it does.
pairs: Makes a new array by transforming every item
Keeps only items that pass a test
Combines all items into one value
True if at least one item passes
True only if all items pass

quiz.why: map applies the function to each element and returns a new array: [10, 20, 30].
filter keeps elements that pass the test. Only 5 and 8 are greater than 4, so the result is [5, 8].
reduce starts at 0 and adds each item: 0 + 3 + 4 = 7.
